topics: Paediatric Assessment and Vital Signs in the Community

questions.question_text: Which statement best describes growth in a child?

choices.text: An increase in the size and number of body cells
The acquisition of social and emotional skills
The improvement of intellectual abilities only
The development of communication and language skills

questions.rationale: Growth refers to measurable physical changes, including increases in height, weight and body size. Development involves the progressive acquisition of functional and behavioural skills.

questions.question_text: Which developmental domain involves a child's ability to understand, learn, remember and solve problems?

choices.text: Gross motor development
Cognitive development
Fine motor development
Social development

questions.rationale: Cognitive development involves mental processes such as thinking, memory, reasoning, learning and problem-solving. These abilities develop progressively from infancy through adolescence.

questions.question_text: At which age does an infant normally begin to demonstrate social smiling?

choices.text: At birth
Around 6 weeks to 2 months
Around 8 months
Around 12 months

questions.rationale: Social smiling commonly emerges during the first two months of life. It is an early social and emotional developmental milestone.

questions.question_text: Which developmental stage is generally associated with Erikson's conflict of autonomy versus shame and doubt?

choices.text: Infancy
Toddlerhood
School age
Adolescence

questions.rationale: Erikson associated autonomy versus shame and doubt with approximately 1–3 years of age. During this period, children develop independence through activities such as feeding and dressing themselves.

questions.question_text: Which measurement is most appropriate for monitoring linear growth in a child younger than two years?

choices.text: Standing height
Recumbent length
Head circumference only
Mid-upper arm circumference only

questions.rationale: Recumbent length is used to measure linear growth in children younger than two years. Children aged two years and above are generally measured standing, provided they can stand correctly.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic of adolescence?

choices.text: Complete dependence on caregivers for all activities
Onset of puberty and development of secondary sexual characteristics
Absence of emotional changes
Cessation of physical growth in all individuals

questions.rationale: Adolescence is characterised by rapid physical, psychological and social changes. Puberty involves hormonal changes and the development of secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.question_text: Which anthropometric measurement is commonly used to screen for acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months in community settings?

choices.text: Head circumference
Mid-upper arm circumference
Chest circumference
Abdominal circumference

questions.rationale: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a practical community screening tool for acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months. It helps identify children who require further assessment and appropriate nutritional intervention.

questions.question_text: Which vaccine is routinely administered at birth under the Expanded Programme on Immunization in Ghana?

choices.text: BCG
Measles-rubella vaccine
Yellow fever vaccine
Pentavalent vaccine

questions.rationale: BCG is administered at birth or as soon as possible thereafter to protect against severe forms of childhood tuberculosis. The birth dose of oral polio vaccine is also included in the routine infant immunization schedule.

questions.question_text: At which age is the first routine dose of measles-rubella vaccine generally scheduled in Ghana?

choices.text: At birth
6 weeks
9 months
18 months

questions.rationale: The first routine measles-rubella dose is scheduled at 9 months under Ghana's routine childhood immunization programme. A second dose is scheduled at 18 months to strengthen protection.

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) strategy?

choices.text: To manage childhood illnesses through an integrated approach at health facility and community levels
To provide treatment exclusively for childhood malaria
To replace routine childhood immunization
To manage only surgical conditions in children

questions.rationale: IMCI is an integrated strategy for improving the prevention, assessment and management of common childhood illnesses. It addresses the child holistically rather than focusing on a single disease.

questions.question_text: Which clinical feature is particularly characteristic of kwashiorkor?

choices.text: Bilateral pitting oedema
Severe dehydration as the defining feature
Excessive accumulation of muscle mass
Increased subcutaneous fat

questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema is a defining clinical feature of kwashiorkor and is an important sign of severe acute malnutrition. Other features may include skin changes, hair changes and poor appetite.

questions.question_text: Which clinical appearance is commonly associated with marasmus?

choices.text: Generalised oedema with a swollen appearance
Severe wasting with marked loss of subcutaneous fat
Excessive weight gain
Enlargement of the limbs due to fluid retention

questions.rationale: Marasmus is characterised by severe wasting resulting from prolonged inadequate energy intake. The child typically has markedly reduced muscle and fat stores and appears extremely thin.

questions.question_text: Which organism causes malaria?

choices.text: Salmonella species
Plasmodium species
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Vibrio cholerae

questions.rationale: Malaria is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Plasmodium. In Ghana, Plasmodium falciparum is the predominant species responsible for malaria infections.

questions.question_text: Which clinical sign is most strongly associated with pneumonia in a child under five years?

choices.text: Fast breathing or lower chest wall indrawing
Increased appetite
Excessive urination
Painless skin discolouration

questions.rationale: Fast breathing and lower chest wall indrawing are important signs used in the assessment of childhood pneumonia. Their presence requires appropriate classification and management under IMCI guidelines.

questions.question_text: Neonatal jaundice refers to yellow discolouration of the skin and sclera caused by increased levels of which substance?

choices.text: Haemoglobin
Bilirubin
Albumin
Creatinine

questions.rationale: Neonatal jaundice results from elevated bilirubin levels in the blood, causing yellow discolouration of the skin and sclera. Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can cause bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction.

questions.question_text: A preterm infant is defined as a baby born before the completion of how many weeks of gestation?

choices.text: 28 weeks
32 weeks
37 completed weeks
40 completed weeks

questions.rationale: A preterm infant is born before 37 completed weeks of gestation. Preterm infants are at increased risk of respiratory, thermal, feeding and infectious complications.

questions.question_text: Which principle is essential when calculating medication doses for children?

choices.text: Using the same adult dose for every child
Calculating the prescribed dose using the child's weight when indicated
Estimating the dose according to the child's appearance
Increasing the dose whenever the child has a fever

questions.rationale: Many paediatric medications are prescribed according to body weight in mg/kg, subject to recommended maximum doses and clinical guidance. Accurate weight measurement and dose verification help prevent medication errors.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse visits a mother whose 9-month-old infant cannot sit without support. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Reassure the mother that all infants develop at exactly the same rate
Assess other developmental milestones and arrange further developmental evaluation
Advise the mother to stop breastfeeding
Conclude immediately that the child has cerebral palsy

questions.rationale: An infant who cannot sit independently around this age requires further developmental assessment. The nurse should evaluate other milestones, growth, health history and possible contributing factors before arranging appropriate referral.

questions.question_text: During a CHPS home visit, a mother reports that her 2-year-old child frequently says 'no' and insists on feeding independently. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

choices.text: Explain that these behaviours may reflect normal autonomy development
Advise the mother to punish the child whenever the child refuses instructions
Recommend preventing the child from attempting independent activities
Explain that the behaviour indicates intellectual disability

questions.rationale: Toddlers commonly demonstrate independence and assertiveness as part of autonomy development. Caregivers should provide safe opportunities for age-appropriate independence while maintaining reasonable boundaries.

questions.question_text: A nurse notices that a 4-year-old child has difficulty using a spoon and cannot copy a simple circle. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Ignore the findings because all children develop at different rates
Assess fine motor development and arrange further evaluation if concerns persist
Immediately diagnose severe intellectual disability
Restrict the child's play activities

questions.rationale: Using a spoon and copying simple shapes involve fine motor and visual-motor coordination skills. The nurse should assess the child's overall development and refer for further evaluation when developmental concerns are identified.

questions.question_text: During a community assessment, a nurse measures the respiratory rate of a calm 18-month-old child and records 48 breaths per minute. How should this finding be interpreted using the IMCI fast-breathing threshold?

choices.text: It is below the fast-breathing threshold
It meets the fast-breathing threshold for a child aged 12 months to 5 years
It indicates normal breathing for every child under five years
It confirms severe pneumonia without further assessment

questions.rationale: For children aged 12 months to 5 years, a respiratory rate of 40 breaths per minute or more meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold. The nurse should assess for chest indrawing, general danger signs and other features before classifying the illness.

questions.question_text: A nurse is assessing a 6-month-old infant at a CHPS compound. Which technique is most appropriate when counting the infant's respiratory rate?

choices.text: Count breaths for 15 seconds while the infant is crying
Count abdominal or chest movements for a full 60 seconds while the infant is calm
Estimate the rate by observing the infant for 5 seconds
Count breaths immediately after feeding without allowing the infant to settle

questions.rationale: Infants have relatively rapid and sometimes irregular breathing, so respiratory rate should be counted for a full minute. The infant should be calm because crying and agitation can increase the respiratory rate.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 3-year-old child to a CHPS compound because the child has fever and poor feeding. Which assessment should the nurse perform first?

choices.text: Assess for general danger signs, including inability to drink, vomiting everything, convulsions and lethargy or unconsciousness
Ask about the child's preferred television programme
Measure the child's height before assessing the general condition
Provide an antipyretic without conducting an assessment

questions.rationale: IMCI assessment begins by checking for general danger signs because they may indicate severe illness requiring urgent attention. A child with a danger sign needs prompt assessment, stabilisation where necessary and urgent referral according to protocol.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 6-week-old infant to a health facility for routine immunization. Which group of vaccines is generally due at this visit under Ghana's EPI schedule?

choices.text: BCG and measles-rubella
Pentavalent 1, OPV 1, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine 1 and rotavirus vaccine 1
Yellow fever and measles-rubella
Only the second dose of measles-rubella vaccine

questions.rationale: At 6 weeks, infants generally receive the first doses of pentavalent, oral polio, pneumococcal conjugate and rotavirus vaccines under the routine schedule. The nurse should verify the current national EPI schedule and the child's immunization record.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 10-week-old infant for immunization. The child received the first routine infant vaccine doses at 6 weeks. Which action is appropriate?

choices.text: Repeat all birth vaccines only
Administer the second scheduled doses of the relevant infant vaccines
Start the measles-rubella vaccination series
Discontinue immunization because the child has already received vaccines

questions.rationale: The 10-week visit is generally the second routine infant immunization contact for vaccines given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. The nurse should check the child's card and administer the due doses according to the national schedule.

questions.question_text: A 9-month-old child attends a child welfare clinic and has no documented measles-rubella or yellow fever vaccination. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Administer the vaccines due at 9 months according to the national EPI schedule
Wait until the child starts school
Give only BCG because it protects against all childhood infections
Advise the mother that these vaccines are unnecessary if the child is healthy

questions.rationale: Measles-rubella and yellow fever vaccines are generally scheduled at 9 months in Ghana's routine immunization programme. The nurse should review the immunization card and administer the due vaccines unless a valid clinical reason prevents vaccination.

questions.question_text: A child missed the scheduled 14-week immunization visit because the family travelled. The mother brings the child to the clinic at 7 months. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Restart the entire immunization schedule from birth
Assess the immunization record and provide appropriate catch-up vaccination
Refuse vaccination because the child is older than 14 weeks
Wait until the child reaches 5 years

questions.rationale: Missed routine immunization doses should generally be addressed through catch-up vaccination rather than restarting the entire series. The nurse must check age-specific eligibility, minimum intervals and national guidance, particularly for vaccines with upper age limits.

questions.question_text: A mother reports mild fever after her infant received routine immunization. What should the community health nurse advise?

choices.text: Mild fever can occur after vaccination; continue observation and provide appropriate care according to guidance
The child has definitely developed a severe vaccine reaction
All future vaccines must be permanently stopped
Give antibiotics immediately without assessing the child

questions.rationale: Mild fever is a recognised adverse event following immunization and usually resolves without serious complications. The caregiver should be advised on appropriate fever management and to seek care if severe or unusual symptoms develop.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 2-year-old child to a CHPS compound with diarrhoea lasting two days. The child is restless, has sunken eyes and drinks eagerly when offered water. How should the nurse classify the child's hydration status?

choices.text: No dehydration
Some dehydration
Severe dehydration
Persistent diarrhoea

questions.rationale: Restlessness, sunken eyes and eager drinking are features used in IMCI to identify some dehydration when the required combination of signs is present. The child should receive the appropriate rehydration plan, usually Plan B, and be reassessed.

questions.question_text: A 10-month-old infant presents with diarrhoea, lethargy, sunken eyes and an inability to drink. What is the most appropriate management?

choices.text: Manage at home with ordinary drinking water only
Urgently manage as severe dehydration and arrange referral or facility-based treatment
Give antidiarrhoeal medication and discharge the infant
Delay treatment until the diarrhoea stops

questions.rationale: Lethargy and inability to drink are general danger signs, and the other findings raise concern for severe dehydration. The nurse should initiate appropriate emergency management, including intravenous rehydration where indicated and feasible under protocol, and arrange urgent referral.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child presents with cough and a respiratory rate of 44 breaths per minute. There is no chest indrawing or general danger sign. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.text: The child meets the IMCI fast-breathing criterion and should be assessed and managed for pneumonia according to protocol
The child has severe pneumonia automatically
The respiratory rate is normal for every child under five years
The child should receive antimalarial medication without further assessment

questions.rationale: For a child aged 12 months to 5 years, a respiratory rate of 40 or more breaths per minute meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold. The nurse should classify the illness using the complete IMCI assessment and provide treatment or referral as indicated.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child is brought to a CHPS compound with fever and a history of convulsions at home. The child is now unconscious. What should the nurse do first?

choices.text: Give oral antimalarial medication and ask the mother to return tomorrow
Recognise a general danger sign, provide immediate emergency care and arrange urgent referral
Give food to improve the child's energy level
Wait for the child to regain consciousness before taking action

questions.rationale: Unconsciousness and a history of convulsions indicate a potentially life-threatening condition. The nurse must prioritise airway, breathing and circulation, manage ongoing convulsions according to protocol and arrange urgent referral.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse identifies a 2-year-old child with bilateral pitting oedema of both feet. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Classify the child as having severe acute malnutrition and arrange urgent assessment and management
Advise the mother to increase the child's water intake only
Reassure the mother that oedema is normal in toddlers
Recommend vigorous exercise to reduce the swelling

questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema is a criterion for severe acute malnutrition in children aged 6–59 months. The child requires prompt clinical assessment to determine whether inpatient or outpatient therapeutic management is appropriate.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 18-month-old child for growth monitoring. The child's weight-for-age is below the expected range on the growth chart. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Assess feeding practices, recent illnesses and growth trends, then counsel and arrange follow-up
Conclude that the child has marasmus without further assessment
Stop all complementary feeding
Ignore the measurement because weight is not useful in children

questions.rationale: A low weight-for-age measurement indicates underweight and requires further assessment of the child's nutritional and health status. The nurse should review the growth trajectory, dietary intake, illness history and other anthropometric indicators before planning interventions.

questions.question_text: A 14-month-old child has severe wasting, prominent ribs and very little subcutaneous fat. There is no bilateral pitting oedema. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?

choices.text: Kwashiorkor
Marasmus
Obesity
Nutritional rickets

questions.rationale: Severe wasting and marked loss of subcutaneous fat without bilateral pitting oedema are characteristic of marasmus. The child requires assessment for complications and appropriate nutritional rehabilitation.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, headache and vomiting at a health facility in a malaria-endemic community. What should the nurse do to support appropriate malaria diagnosis?

choices.text: Diagnose malaria based on fever alone
Arrange a malaria parasitological test using an approved rapid diagnostic test or microscopy
Prescribe antibiotics without assessment
Assume the child has measles

questions.rationale: Fever alone is not sufficient to confirm malaria because many childhood illnesses cause fever. Parasitological confirmation using an approved rapid diagnostic test or microscopy is recommended before antimalarial treatment, except where emergency clinical protocols require immediate action.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 2-year-old child with acute diarrhoea to a CHPS compound. The child is alert and has no signs of dehydration. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Continue feeding and breastfeeding, give extra fluids and administer ORS and zinc according to guidelines
Stop breastfeeding until the diarrhoea resolves
Give antibiotics for every episode of diarrhoea
Withhold all fluids for 12 hours

questions.rationale: Children with diarrhoea and no dehydration should receive extra fluids, continued feeding and breastfeeding, and zinc supplementation according to national guidance. ORS should be given to replace ongoing fluid losses and caregivers should be taught danger signs.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child has fever, cough, red eyes and a widespread rash that began on the face and spread downwards. Which illness should the nurse suspect?

choices.text: Measles
Kwashiorkor
Tetanus
Acute gastroenteritis

questions.rationale: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a maculopapular rash spreading from the face downwards are characteristic features of measles. The nurse should follow infection prevention procedures, assess for complications and report and refer according to public health guidance.

questions.question_text: A child with suspected pneumonia is brought to a CHPS compound. The nurse observes severe respiratory distress and central cyanosis. What is the priority action?

choices.text: Give cough syrup and discharge the child
Provide emergency supportive care, including oxygen if indicated and available, and arrange urgent referral
Advise the mother to use herbal preparations
Schedule a routine review in one week

questions.rationale: Central cyanosis and severe respiratory distress indicate a potentially life-threatening respiratory condition. The nurse should prioritise airway and breathing support, provide oxygen where indicated and arrange immediate referral to an appropriate facility.

questions.question_text: A mother brings her 3-day-old newborn to a CHPS compound because the baby's skin appears yellow. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Assess the newborn promptly and arrange appropriate bilirubin evaluation or referral
Reassure the mother that all jaundice is harmless
Advise the mother to stop breastfeeding
Recommend exposing the newborn to direct midday sunlight as the only treatment

questions.rationale: Neonatal jaundice requires assessment because significant hyperbilirubinaemia can cause neurological injury. The nurse should establish the age of onset, assess the baby's general condition and arrange bilirubin measurement or referral according to the clinical findings.

questions.question_text: A newborn is delivered at 34 weeks of gestation and has difficulty maintaining body temperature. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?

choices.text: Provide thermal care, preferably skin-to-skin kangaroo mother care when clinically appropriate
Bathe the newborn immediately in cold water
Leave the newborn uncovered to improve skin ventilation
Place the newborn near an open window

questions.rationale: Preterm infants have reduced ability to regulate body temperature and are at high risk of hypothermia. Kangaroo mother care, appropriate wrapping and temperature monitoring help maintain warmth and improve outcomes.

questions.question_text: A mother reports that her 5-day-old newborn has stopped breastfeeding and feels unusually cold. The baby is also less active than usual. What should the community health nurse suspect?

choices.text: Normal newborn behaviour
Possible neonatal sepsis or another serious neonatal illness
Normal teething
Uncomplicated colic

questions.rationale: Poor feeding, hypothermia and reduced activity are danger signs in a newborn and may indicate neonatal sepsis. The nurse should arrange urgent assessment and referral without delaying for home treatment.

questions.question_text: A mother has delivered a healthy newborn at a health facility. Which practice best supports the prevention of neonatal hypothermia immediately after birth?

choices.text: Dry the newborn thoroughly, remove wet cloths and provide skin-to-skin contact
Delay drying until after the first bath
Place the newborn on a cold surface
Separate the newborn from the mother without clinical indication

questions.rationale: Immediate drying and skin-to-skin contact reduce heat loss after birth. Delayed bathing, appropriate wrapping and early breastfeeding further support thermal protection.

questions.question_text: A child weighs 12 kg and is prescribed a medicine at 10 mg/kg per dose. What is the correct amount of medicine for one dose?

choices.text: 12 mg
22 mg
120 mg

questions.rationale: The prescribed dose is calculated by multiplying the child's weight by the dose per kilogram: 12 kg × 10 mg/kg = 120 mg. The nurse must also verify the medication concentration, route, frequency and maximum recommended dose.

questions.question_text: A nurse is preparing an oral liquid medicine for a child. Which equipment is most appropriate for measuring the prescribed dose accurately?

choices.text: A household tablespoon
A calibrated oral syringe
A drinking glass
An unmarked bottle cap

questions.rationale: A calibrated oral syringe allows accurate measurement of small liquid medication volumes. Household spoons and bottle caps are unreliable because their volumes vary.

questions.question_text: A caregiver tells the community health nurse that the child vomited shortly after taking an oral medication. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Automatically repeat the full dose
Assess the medication, timing and amount vomited, then follow the relevant clinical guidance before deciding on another dose
Double the next dose
Stop all medication permanently

questions.rationale: Whether a dose should be repeated depends on the medicine, the time elapsed and the circumstances of vomiting. Automatically repeating or doubling a dose may cause toxicity, so the nurse should follow medicine-specific guidance or consult an appropriate prescriber.

questions.question_text: A 13-year-old boy tells a community health nurse that he feels uncomfortable because his voice is changing and he is growing taller rapidly. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Explain that these changes may be normal features of puberty and provide age-appropriate guidance
Tell him that these changes indicate a disease
Advise him to avoid physical activity until growth stops
Tell him that puberty occurs only in girls

questions.rationale: Voice changes and rapid height increase are common features of male puberty. The nurse should provide accurate information, promote healthy self-image and encourage the adolescent to discuss concerns openly.

questions.question_text: A mother refuses to allow her 9-month-old child to receive measles-rubella vaccine because she believes the vaccine causes measles. Which response by the nurse is best?

choices.text: Explain that the vaccine stimulates immunity against measles and rubella and discuss possible mild adverse reactions
Tell the mother that vaccination is unnecessary if the child has never had measles
Threaten the mother with punishment
Agree that the vaccine causes measles and advise against it

questions.rationale: The measles-rubella vaccine protects against two important viral infections by stimulating an immune response. Clear, respectful health education can address misconceptions and support informed vaccination decisions.

questions.question_text: A child with suspected measles is brought to a crowded CHPS compound. Which action should the nurse take to reduce the risk of transmission?

choices.text: Place the child in a separate area and apply appropriate infection prevention precautions
Allow the child to play with other children in the waiting area
Encourage other children to share the child's drinking cup
Delay all infection prevention measures until laboratory confirmation

questions.rationale: Measles is highly contagious and spreads through airborne transmission. Suspected cases should be separated promptly, with appropriate respiratory infection prevention measures and notification according to public health procedures.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child has diarrhoea for 15 days but is alert and able to drink. What is the appropriate IMCI classification?

choices.text: Acute watery diarrhoea only
Persistent diarrhoea
Severe dehydration automatically
Dysentery

questions.rationale: Diarrhoea lasting 14 days or longer is classified as persistent diarrhoea under IMCI. The nurse should assess hydration and nutritional status and arrange appropriate management or referral.

questions.question_text: During a community growth-monitoring session, a nurse notices that a child's weight has remained unchanged over three consecutive monthly visits. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

choices.text: The child is necessarily growing normally
The child may have growth faltering and requires assessment of feeding, illness and growth history
The child should immediately be diagnosed with kwashiorkor
Growth monitoring should be discontinued

questions.rationale: Failure to gain weight over successive measurements may indicate growth faltering, even if the child does not yet appear visibly malnourished. The nurse should investigate feeding difficulties, recurrent illness and other causes and arrange appropriate intervention.

questions.question_text: A nurse is assessing a 4-month-old infant with cough. The infant has a respiratory rate of 58 breaths per minute while calm. How should the nurse interpret this measurement?

choices.text: It is below the IMCI fast-breathing threshold for this age group
It meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold for an infant aged 2 months to 12 months
It confirms severe pneumonia without any other assessment
It is a normal respiratory rate for all infants

questions.rationale: For infants aged 2 months to 12 months, a respiratory rate of 50 breaths per minute or more meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold. The nurse must assess other clinical signs and classify the illness using the complete IMCI algorithm.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child is brought to a CHPS compound with diarrhoea and visible blood in the stool. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

choices.text: Dysentery
Uncomplicated constipation
Kwashiorkor
Simple viral cough

questions.rationale: Blood in the stool in a child with diarrhoea is a key feature of dysentery under IMCI classification. The child requires assessment and appropriate treatment according to national guidelines.

questions.question_text: A community health nurse is counselling a mother whose 7-month-old infant has recently started complementary feeding. Which advice is most appropriate?

choices.text: Provide safe, adequate and nutrient-dense complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding
Stop breastfeeding immediately after introducing complementary foods
Give only thin maize water until the child is 2 years old
Avoid all animal-source foods throughout infancy

questions.rationale: Complementary feeding should begin at around 6 months while breastfeeding continues. Foods should be age-appropriate, sufficiently frequent, nutrient-dense and prepared hygienically to support growth and development.

questions.question_text: A newborn delivered at home is brought to a CHPS compound. The baby is breathing irregularly and has poor muscle tone. What should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Assess breathing and circulation and initiate appropriate newborn resuscitation steps if indicated
Begin routine weighing before assessing the baby's condition
Give the newborn oral water
Delay assessment until the mother has completed registration

questions.rationale: Irregular breathing and poor tone may indicate neonatal compromise requiring immediate intervention. The nurse should rapidly assess the newborn and initiate resuscitation according to the approved newborn resuscitation protocol and available training.

questions.question_text: A nurse is about to administer an oral medication to a 5-year-old child. The medication label and prescription show different strengths. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Choose the strength that is easiest to measure
Withhold administration until the discrepancy is clarified with the prescriber or pharmacist
Administer both strengths to ensure the child receives enough medicine
Ask the caregiver to select the correct strength

questions.rationale: A discrepancy between the prescription and medication label creates a risk of medication error. The nurse must clarify the correct medicine and strength before administration.

questions.question_text: During a home visit, a nurse finds a 2-year-old child who is breathing rapidly, has severe chest indrawing and is unable to drink. What is the nurse's priority action?

choices.text: Provide routine health education and schedule a visit next month
Recognise severe illness, provide immediate supportive care and arrange urgent referral
Advise the caregiver to give cough syrup and observe for three days
Perform growth monitoring before addressing the respiratory condition

questions.rationale: Severe chest indrawing and inability to drink are concerning findings, with inability to drink being an IMCI general danger sign. Immediate assessment, supportive care and urgent referral take priority over routine community services.

questions.question_text: A 20-month-old child has bilateral pitting oedema, flaky-paint skin changes and sparse, discoloured hair. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: The child has uncomplicated marasmus
The findings are consistent with kwashiorkor, a form of severe acute malnutrition
The child has simple vitamin C deficiency
The child has normal nutritional status

questions.rationale: Bilateral pitting oedema together with characteristic skin and hair changes strongly suggests kwashiorkor. The child requires urgent assessment for complications and appropriate therapeutic nutritional management.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child has fever, cough, fast breathing and a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test. The child also has lower chest wall indrawing. Which approach is most appropriate?

choices.text: Treat malaria only because the positive test explains all the symptoms
Assess and manage both malaria and possible severe respiratory illness, prioritising emergency care and referral as indicated
Ignore the positive malaria test and treat only the cough
Give antipyretics only and discharge the child

questions.rationale: A positive malaria test does not exclude concurrent pneumonia or another serious illness. Lower chest wall indrawing requires careful IMCI classification, and the nurse must address all identified conditions while prioritising respiratory compromise and urgent referral when indicated.

questions.question_text: A child aged 18 months attends a child welfare clinic. The immunization card shows that the child received the first measles-rubella dose at 9 months but missed the scheduled second dose. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Administer the second measles-rubella dose according to the national schedule
Repeat the first dose and cancel the second dose
Wait until the child is 5 years old
Refuse vaccination because the child missed the scheduled date

questions.rationale: The second measles-rubella dose is scheduled at 18 months to provide additional protection. A missed appointment should be addressed through appropriate catch-up vaccination rather than excluding the child from immunization.

questions.question_text: A newborn develops jaundice within the first 24 hours after birth. The mother says that her older child also had jaundice and suggests waiting at home. What is the best nursing decision?

choices.text: Reassure the mother because early jaundice is always physiological
Arrange urgent medical evaluation because jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours is pathological until assessed
Advise the mother to stop breastfeeding for 48 hours
Recommend sunlight exposure and review after one week

questions.rationale: Jaundice developing within the first 24 hours is a significant warning sign and may indicate haemolysis, infection or another serious condition. Prompt bilirubin assessment and clinical evaluation are essential to prevent complications such as acute bilirubin encephalopathy.

questions.question_text: A child weighs 15 kg and is prescribed a medicine at 15 mg/kg/day in three equally divided doses. How much should the child receive per dose?

choices.text: 75 mg
150 mg
225 mg
450 mg

questions.rationale: The total daily dose is 15 kg × 15 mg/kg/day = 225 mg per day. Dividing 225 mg by three equal doses gives 75 mg per dose.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child presents with diarrhoea. The child is lethargic, has sunken eyes and is unable to drink. The caregiver requests immediate discharge because the family has no money for transport. What should the nurse prioritise?

choices.text: Discharge the child and advise the caregiver to purchase ORS later
Explain the severity, initiate emergency management and activate available referral support
Wait until the caregiver obtains money before starting treatment
Provide only dietary advice and arrange a routine follow-up

questions.rationale: Lethargy and inability to drink are general danger signs, and the child may have severe dehydration requiring urgent treatment. The nurse should not delay emergency care because of financial barriers but should use available referral and community support mechanisms.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old adolescent tells a nurse that friends are pressuring him to engage in unprotected sexual activity. He is worried about discussing the issue with his parents. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

choices.text: Scold the adolescent for discussing sexual health
Provide confidential, age-appropriate counselling within applicable safeguarding and consent requirements
Ignore the concern because adolescents cannot make health decisions
Encourage the adolescent to follow the decisions of his friends

questions.rationale: Adolescents need accurate, non-judgemental sexual and reproductive health information and support to make informed decisions. Confidentiality should be respected within legal and safeguarding requirements, including situations involving abuse or immediate risk of harm.

questions.question_text: During a measles outbreak investigation, a community health nurse identifies an unvaccinated child who has fever, cough and conjunctivitis but no rash yet. What is the most appropriate action?

choices.text: Exclude measles because a rash has not appeared
Consider suspected measles based on the exposure and symptoms, isolate appropriately and notify public health authorities according to protocol
Allow the child to attend school until a rash develops
Administer antibiotics and end the investigation

questions.rationale: Measles may initially present with a prodromal phase involving fever, cough and conjunctivitis before the rash appears. During an outbreak, suspected cases require prompt infection prevention measures, clinical assessment and public health notification.

questions.question_text: A 2-day-old newborn has poor feeding, fever, fast breathing and reduced activity. The mother reports that the membranes ruptured more than 24 hours before delivery. Which condition should be strongly suspected?

choices.text: Neonatal sepsis
Normal neonatal adaptation
Physiological weight loss only
Uncomplicated infantile colic

questions.rationale: Poor feeding, temperature instability, fast breathing and reduced activity are concerning signs of neonatal infection. Prolonged rupture of membranes may increase the risk of neonatal sepsis, requiring urgent hospital assessment and treatment.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child has a MUAC of 10.8 cm, bilateral pitting oedema and poor appetite. Which management decision is most appropriate?

choices.text: Manage the child with routine growth monitoring only
Recognise severe acute malnutrition with complications and arrange urgent facility-based assessment and management
Advise the caregiver to give only fruit juice at home
Discharge the child because oedema makes MUAC unreliable

questions.rationale: A MUAC below 11.5 cm in a child aged 6–59 months indicates severe acute malnutrition, and bilateral pitting oedema independently confirms severe acute malnutrition. Poor appetite suggests a complication requiring urgent assessment for inpatient therapeutic care.

questions.question_text: A nurse assesses two children at a CHPS compound. Child A is 8 months old with a respiratory rate of 52 breaths per minute, while Child B is 3 years old with a respiratory rate of 38 breaths per minute. Both have cough. Which interpretation is correct?

choices.text: Both children meet the IMCI fast-breathing threshold
Only Child A meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold
Only Child B meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold
Neither child meets the IMCI fast-breathing threshold

questions.rationale: The fast-breathing threshold is 50 breaths per minute or more for children aged 2–12 months and 40 or more for children aged 12 months to 5 years. Child A meets the threshold, while Child B does not.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child with diarrhoea has received ORS at home, but the caregiver reports that the child is becoming increasingly weak and is no longer able to drink. What should the nurse conclude?

choices.text: The child is recovering because the diarrhoea may be reducing
The child may be developing severe dehydration and requires urgent reassessment and referral
The child should stop all fluids permanently
The child only requires routine vitamin supplementation

questions.rationale: Increasing weakness and inability to drink are danger signs that may indicate severe dehydration or deterioration. The nurse should reassess immediately, initiate appropriate emergency management and arrange urgent referral.

questions.question_text: A nurse calculates a child's prescribed medication dose and finds that it exceeds the recommended maximum daily dose for the medicine. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Administer the calculated dose because weight-based calculations are always correct
Withhold administration and clarify the prescription with the prescriber or pharmacist
Reduce the dose by half without informing anyone
Ask the caregiver to decide the dose

questions.rationale: Weight-based calculations must always be checked against the medicine's recommended maximum dose and relevant clinical guidance. A dose that exceeds the maximum requires clarification before administration to prevent toxicity.

questions.question_text: During a community outreach session, a mother presents an immunization card showing that her 10-month-old child has received BCG and the three primary infant vaccine visits but has no record of the 9-month vaccines. What should the nurse do?

choices.text: Assess the child's immunization history and administer eligible missed vaccines according to catch-up guidance
Restart the entire immunization schedule
Refuse vaccination because the child has passed 9 months
Give only BCG again

questions.rationale: A missed immunization appointment should be addressed by reviewing the child's record and providing eligible catch-up doses. The nurse must consider age limits and minimum intervals for individual vaccines and follow current national EPI guidance.
